draft.title: Medieval law and punishment
card: In medieval Europe, courts often could not find out the truth from evidence. Many people believed God would show who was guilty.
the accused faced a painful test, such as carrying hot iron or being put in water. Surviving or healing well was taken as a sign of innocence.
the accused and the accuser fought each other. People believed God would give victory to the one telling the truth.
Punishments were public and harsh, such as whipping, the stocks or hanging. They were meant to shame the guilty and scare others into obeying the law.
draft.remember: Medieval justice trusted God to reveal the guilty, and punished them in public.

a.q: Why did people in medieval Europe use trial by combat to decide guilt?
opts: They believed God would let the person in the right win
They believed the stronger fighter was likely to be guilty
They believed a fight would make people confess their crimes
They believed a fight was a cheap way to cover court costs
a.why: People believed God would protect the innocent, so the winner was seen as the one telling the truth. The belief was about God's judgement, not about strength or confessions.
a.clue: Think about who people believed was watching over the result.

b.q: In a medieval village, a man accused of theft is made to carry a hot iron, and his hand is checked days later. Which best explains this method?
opts: The result was read as a sign from God about his guilt
The result was used to find out how much he had stolen
The result was a punishment given after he was found guilty
The result was a test of whether he could pay a fine
b.why: Trial by ordeal was used to decide guilt, because people believed God would protect an innocent person. It came before a verdict, so it was not the punishment. The tempting answer, punishment, mixes up how guilt was decided with what happened afterwards.
b.clue: Was the test used before or after guilt was decided?

a.best: They believed God would let the person in the right win

b.best: The result was read as a sign from God about his guilt

problems.detail: 'Being put in water... Surviving... was taken as a sign of innocence' is misleading. In the cold-water ordeal, sinking was read as innocence and floating as guilt, and the accused was usually pulled out alive either way. In the hot-water ordeal, the healing of the scalded hand was checked. The card suggests survival itself was the test, which is a common misconception.

The remember line says medieval justice simply 'trusted God to reveal the guilty'. The card is more careful: courts 'often' could not find the truth from evidence, and 'many people believed' God would show guilt. The line overgeneralises and could suggest that all medieval justice worked this way.

proposal.title: Medieval law and punishment
card: In medieval Europe, courts often could not find out the truth from evidence. Many people believed God would show who was guilty.
the accused faced a painful test before any verdict, such as carrying a hot iron. The hand was bandaged, and if it healed cleanly after a few days, this was taken as a sign of innocence.
the accused and the accuser fought each other. People believed God would give victory to the one telling the truth.
Once someone was found guilty, punishments were public and harsh, such as whipping, the stocks or hanging. They were meant to shame the guilty and scare others into obeying the law.
proposal.remember: Ordeal and combat rested on a belief that God would protect the innocent. Punishment came after, and it was public and harsh.
